description: L-SEA is a two-person team from Málaga: Rafael and Marcos. We built L-SEA for the NASA Space Apps Challenge Málaga 2026 to make lunar south-pole landing-site planning understandable and reproducible. Between us we covered the scientific core, NASA data pipeline, 3D/2D interface, testing, security and deployment. The project is open source under MIT, and our goal is a transparent tool that helps planners and educators compare sites and dates with real NASA data.
summary: L-SEA is a browser-based tool for comparing lunar south-pole landing sites and dates, built for the NASA Space Apps Challenge Málaga 2026 and challenge 10, "Lunar Landing Site Navigator". Landing on the Moon's south pole means trading sunlight for power, Earth visibility for direct communications, and terrain that hides the horizon. Mission planners face these trade-offs whenever a launch date or landing site changes, but the data sits in tools built for specialists. Our design puts site selection, Sun and Earth positions relative to the horizon, time to sunset or earthset, power and communications windows, and an autopilot site scorer in one interface for mission planners and educators, with a bilingual EN/ES UI and a JSON mission-brief export. The repository ships real NASA LOLA terrain and uses pre-computed JPL Horizons ephemerides so it runs as a static site, with a 2D fallback for machines without WebGL.
details:
L-SEA is a browser-based mission-planning console for the lunar south pole. It combines real LOLA elevation data, precomputed JPL Horizons topocentric Sun/Earth ephemerides and a configurable mission profile into a single analysis workflow. The user selects a DEM region, a curated site or an automatically detected landing zone, and the application ray-traces the local terrain horizon before computing illumination, solar/RTG power, eclipse battery requirements, thermal equilibrium, direct and relay communications, slope and crater hazards, and an overall feasibility verdict. A deterministic autopilot detects contiguous flat zones, applies hard feasibility gates (continuous sunlight, battery sized to the longest eclipse, power margin, thermal, data budget) and ranks them by a documented weighted score. It can also search the 2026-11-01 to 2026-12-31 ephemeris window for each zone's earliest feasible mission start date, so users are not required to guess a date manually.

Benefits. The tool replaces a manual workflow across JPL Horizons, Moon Trek, LROC QuickMap and spreadsheets. It shows why a site is or is not viable, rather than only a score: terrain shadowing, eclipse duration, power deficit, thermal limits and communication gaps are exposed with units and provenance. Results are reproducible through an input signature, exportable as a JSON mission brief, and available in English and Spanish. The interface runs entirely in the browser, with computation in a Web Worker and a Canvas 2D fallback when WebGL is unavailable.

Intended impact. L-SEA supports mission planners, researchers, students and the public in understanding the trade-offs of landing and operating near the lunar south pole. It makes illumination, power and communication constraints tangible, encourages evidence-based site comparison and provides a transparent, auditable alternative to black-box scoring. The same architecture can be extended to other polar datasets or mission profiles.

Tools, languages and hardware. JavaScript (ES modules), CSS and HTML for the front end; Vue 3 and Three.js for the interface and 3D/2D terrain; Vite for the build; vue-i18n for bilingual copy; Vitest for 243 unit and contract tests; a Web Worker for background computation; Python 3 with rasterio and NumPy for DEM cropping/resampling; Node.js for data and QA scripts; headless Google Chrome with the Chrome DevTools Protocol for end-to-end and responsive testing; GitHub Actions and GitHub Pages for CI and static deployment; Miro REST API through a local Model Context Protocol server for project planning. A declared AI coding assistant was used for development support. The application runs on standard laptops and desktops; WebGL is optional because the 2D fallback covers devices without it. No custom hardware or backend server is required.

Creativity. The core idea is terrain-first rather than ephemeris-only: the local horizon is ray-traced from real elevation data, so a ridge that hides the Sun or Earth changes the result. That physical model is combined with hard mission-feasibility gates, automatic feasible-date search, side-by-side 3D and top-down 2D views, visual Sun/link cycle strips, a site comparator, historical mission presets and an exportable brief. The autopilot is deliberately deterministic and documented, not a black box.

Factors considered. We prioritised real NASA data and provenance over synthetic values; honest feasibility over attractive scores; explicit limits (DEM resolution, two-month ephemeris coverage, planning estimates rather than flight certification); performance and payload (lazy DEM loading, cached horizon profiles, worker offloading); accessibility and the event UX guide (contrast, target sizes, empty/loading/error states); EN/ES parity; and reproducibility through tests, signatures and documented assumptions.
